The investigation stalled. Within a month I was moved off the key client I'd handled for two years. My manager started copying HR into every email she sent me, as if I were the problem. I'd go home and sit in the dark without switching on the lights. I'm Kiran, and I'd never felt so alone in a building full of people I knew.

In the small flat in Kraków, Olga sat at her desk, homework untouched, replaying the scene from Friday. Oskar, her friend since primary school, had read her private poem aloud at the class party, in a silly voice, after she'd shown it to him in confidence.
She had rehearsed a hundred replies since then. Clever ones. Cruel ones. On the tram she imagined posting his embarrassing childhood photos where everyone would see, or telling the whole class about his fear of the dark. She could picture exactly how his face would look.
For a few seconds each fantasy felt like power. Then she'd look up and realise she'd missed her tram stop, or read the same page of chemistry four times.
Her mother knocked. "You've been quiet all weekend."
"I'm fine," Olga said, but her jaw was tight. Oskar had probably forgotten the whole thing by now. She, meanwhile, was carrying it everywhere.

qa.q: What did Oskar read aloud at the class party?
qa.a: Her private poem, in a silly voice.

qa.q: What does Olga feel during each revenge fantasy?
qa.a: She feels a brief burst of power, then distracted and tense as the hurt stays fresh.

qa.q: What could Olga do instead of rehearsing payback?
qa.a: Tell her mother what happened, and decide calmly whether to tell Oskar how it felt, so the event stops living in her head.

qa.a: Oskar may have moved on without realising how much he hurt Olga, or feel uneasy but unsure how to apologise.

grounding: A teen replays a friend's betrayal and rehearses revenge, which feels powerful but keeps her stuck and distracted.

In the hostel study hall of her boarding school in Ooty, Vidya stared at her physics book without seeing it. Two weeks ago Thomas, who she'd trusted with everything, had told the whole dorm that she'd cried after failing the maths test. Now people called her "Tears" in the corridor.
Every night after lights out she replayed it. She rehearsed the argument she'd have with him, perfect sentences, crushing ones. She imagined telling the warden it was Thomas who broke the lab window last term. She imagined him being sent home, and everyone knowing.
In the moment, the plans made her feel strong. Afterwards, she felt worse. Her marks were slipping. She'd stopped going to choir, because Thomas was in it.
Tonight, when her roommate asked if she wanted to go for hot chocolate, Vidya said no, and went back to rehearsing. She realised, with a tired kind of shock, that Thomas was still in charge of her evenings.

qa.a: Tears.

qa.a: She feels drained and stuck, realising the replaying lets Thomas control her evenings.

For a month Harish had been furious with Lavanya. She had been his best friend through three years of engineering college, and she'd told the placement cell about the internship offer he was quietly considering, so that she could apply for it first. She got it.
He'd ranted to everyone. He'd deleted her photos. He'd written long messages and not sent them.
Then one evening in the canteen, a song came on that they used to sing badly on bus trips, and Harish found his eyes filling. Not with rage. With something heavier.
He went back to his room and sat on the bed. It wasn't just the internship. It was the late-night chai, the notes she used to save for him, the way she laughed at his terrible jokes. The picture he'd had of her, someone who'd never do this, was gone.
He cried properly for the first time. Afterwards he felt emptier, but also lighter, as if a knot had begun to loosen.

qa.a: She got the internship.

qa.q: What did Harish feel when the song played?
qa.a: He felt a heavy grief beneath the anger, for the lost friendship and the picture he had of Lavanya.

qa.q: Why is letting himself cry a step forward for Harish?
qa.a: Feeling the sadness instead of covering it with fury lets the grief move, loosening the knot.

grounding: Beneath a month of fury at a friend's betrayal, a young man finds grief for the lost friendship, and feeling it begins to move him forward.

"You've barely eaten, Suraj," his mother said, sitting beside him on the steps.
"I'm not hungry. I'm angry. Varun told the whole team about my brother's arrest. I told him in confidence, Amma. He was my best friend."
"I know. You've told me."
"Three times, I know." Suraj kicked a pebble. "I keep planning what I'll say to him. How I'll make him feel as small as I did."
"And does it help?"

"So you've lost that."
"Yeah." His eyes filled. "I miss him, Amma. Isn't that stupid? I'm furious and I miss him."
She put her arm around him. "It's not stupid. That's grief. Let it come."

I let myself be sad that whole afternoon, instead of reaching for the anger. Strangely, by evening, I felt a little lighter.
I'm Gopika, and I think that afternoon was when the healing actually started.

The Howrah express was four hours late, and the only empty seat in the crowded sleeper coach was opposite Gopika, the college friend who had spread the rumour that cost Abhinav his place as student secretary last year.
They sat in stiff silence for two hours. Then, somewhere past Asansol, with the lights flickering, Gopika spoke. "I was scared that year. My scholarship depended on the student council's recommendation, and the other group promised me theirs if I helped them. I told myself the rumour was half true."
Abhinav wanted to say, that's no excuse. It wasn't. But he watched her twist the strap of her bag, and remembered her mother was a cook at the hostel, and that the scholarship was everything.
"It was still wrong," he said.
"I know," she said. "I've known for a year."
He didn't forgive her on the train. But as they reached Howrah in the grey dawn, the bitterness he had carried felt a little less heavy.

qa.a: His place as student secretary last year.

Tanuja had not spoken to her older brother Jagdish since he took the gold chain their grandmother left her and pawned it. Six months of silence, even at Diwali.
Then her cousin let something slip at a wedding: Jagdish had lost his job in March and hadn't told anyone. He'd been paying rent with borrowed money and was too ashamed to face their father, who had always called him the failure of the family.
That night Tanuja lay awake. She pictured Jagdish, twenty-three, alone in his rented room in Nagpur, terrified, taking the one thing he knew he could sell. It didn't make it right.
But the anger, which had felt like a hard stone in her chest, softened a little around the edges. He wasn't a villain. He was a scared young man who had made a bad, cowardly choice.
She still didn't call him. Not yet. But she stopped rehearsing the speech about how he'd always been selfish.

I've been Chinmay's friend since school, so I've heard the story more times than I can count: how his business partner, Rakesh, took their biggest client and walked out. I've heard it over chai, on the phone at midnight, in the car. Each time the same details, the same bitterness.
The first few times, I told him to let it go. He went silent, and I could see he felt dismissed.
So I changed. Last Friday, when he started again, I just listened, all the way through. I didn't interrupt, didn't advise. When he finished, I asked, quietly, "What do you want now, Chinmay? Not about Rakesh. For you."
He looked startled. He was quiet for a long time. Then he said, "I want to stop thinking about him every morning. I want to start something of my own."
I don't know what was going on inside him. But it was the first time the story ended with something other than Rakesh.

qa.q: What did Rakesh take when he walked out?
qa.a: Their biggest client.

qa.q: What did the narrator feel after telling Chinmay to let it go?
qa.a: The narrator felt uneasy and regretful, seeing that the advice made Chinmay feel dismissed.

qa.q: Why did asking 'What do you want now?' help?
qa.a: After being fully heard, Chinmay could turn from the bitter story toward his own future.

qa.q: What might Chinmay have felt when asked what he wants?
qa.a: Chinmay was likely startled and then a little hopeful, shifting from resentment to thinking about his own next step.

First weekend. Lalit told Jyoti again how his cousin had lied to the family about the land and got their grandmother's house. Jyoti said, "You should just forgive him and move on, yaar." Lalit's face shut like a door. He changed the subject.
Second weekend. The story came back, angrier. This time Jyoti bit her tongue. She let him talk for forty minutes without offering a single solution. She nodded, asked what he'd felt when he found out, and let the silence sit.
Third weekend. Lalit told it once more, but shorter. When he finished, Jyoti asked gently, "What do you actually want now? Not from him. For yourself."
Lalit stared at his tea. "I want to stop feeling like a fool every time I pass that street. Maybe I want to talk to Dadi about it, just once."
Jyoti felt a small relief. For the first time in weeks, he was talking about what came next.

qa.q: What did Lalit's cousin get?
qa.a: Their grandmother's house.

qa.q: What did Jyoti feel when Lalit started talking about what came next?
qa.a: Jyoti felt a small relief, seeing Lalit finally look forward instead of only back.

qa.a: Being fully heard made Lalit feel respected, so a gentle question about what he wants could open a way forward.

Omkar, you keep telling me about your friend who won't stop talking about the colleague who betrayed him. Let me tell you about Bashir and me, Yusuf, when we were twenty.
Bashir's elder brother had cheated him out of their father's cycle shop. For a whole year, every evening on the riverbank in Srinagar, Bashir told me the story again. The same words. The same fury.
I was young and impatient. One evening I said, "Enough, forgive him, it's done." Bashir walked away and didn't speak to me for a week. I had made him feel his pain was a nuisance.
When he came back, I tried something different. I just listened, the whole story, without a word. Then I asked, "Bashir, what do you want for yourself now?" He was silent a long time. Then he said, "My own shop. Not his."
Two years later he opened one. That question did more than all my advice. So, beta: listen first. Then ask.

qa.a: Their father's cycle shop.

qa.a: Yusuf felt regretful and chastened, realising the impatient advice had made Bashir feel his pain was a nuisance.

qa.a: Listening to the whole story without a word, then asking what Bashir wanted for himself, which led him toward his own shop.

qa.a: Bashir probably felt heard and respected, able at last to think about his own future.
